These two things go hand in hand for me. What I buy for food is directly driven by the meals I'm preparing. Another way to say this is that I only buy what's needed for the meals I'm going to prepare. This means a menu first, then a shopping list (after doing inventory of the pantry, fridge and freezer). This Also ties into general health as diet is easily the lions share of looking and feeling good.

So, sales fliers are published on Wednesdays here and I can see them online. The first step is always to check those flier to see what's on sale. Easily 95% of the stuff for sale are name brands (which I don't generally buy) and/or pre-prepared food (which I never buy). But I look to see the meat, veggie and dairy sales and this drives my meals for the week. Since my wife works Wed~Fri, it's also great timing for me to get myself to the store, which is 2 hours round trip of driving plus whatever time I spend in the stores. Welcome to the boonies and cheap rural living... :) I pay a different price for being able to buy nice houses for $60k. One thing I don't really do is coupon, my main store where I do 80~90% of my shopping doesn't have them (Aldi, if you have one near don't be too proud to try it out as their "generic" food is better than most name brand stuff ~ plus who can complain about $0.19/dozen eggs? ), but even before that I don't get anything where coupons are delivered (newspapers), and found that the lions share of coupons were for brand name stuff that was more expensive than generic even after the savings. I understand that some stores do double/stacking, but my Backup store (where I get the remaining few items not found at Aldi) is Kroger and they don't double/stack if it's over $1. So I've never bothered with coupons beyond loading the few freebies Kroger sends to my digital account/card.

So, this week it looks like beef and pork tenderloin (the beef is "filet mignon" once cut, heh), a frozen pot-roast kit (yuck), chicken and a steak. The veggie is asparagus.. thin pickings on that front in the winter. :) Front page is really all the further I look as those are the "cost leaders", which are basically the good deals used to get you in the store. Everything else (again, I look at meat, veggie and dairy) tends to be so close to normal pricing as to not really be worth the time to look time, I still do but don't drive my shopping based on it. And in all truth, Aldi prices tend to be below the best prices Kroger can offer anyway.

So, knowing what's on sale I then reference my recipes. I use Pepperplate as an app for my tablet in the kitchen and on the web with my laptop in the living room (don't do smartphones, thank you very much). I've spent a good bit of time organizing and labeling the hundreds of recipes that make it into my collection, so I can simply pull up all entries with "pork" as a label, or "steak" ~ I have lots of labels since there's no limit and I can easily cross-reference. I can usually come up with 3~4 meals based on the sales and then ask my wife if she has any cravings. She's been craving mexician type foods a lot lately, but it changes and I like to make sure I scratch those itches. I also try hard to make sure one meal a week is vegetarian , this is simply for our own personal health but it is a consideration for the shopping list/meal plan.

I won't bore you with my specific list, but mention that I know my two stores Very well. I know what's on every isle and my path through the stores and layout my list so I hit the store in the most efficient route possible. Maybe silly, but it's hardly any extra effort. Then there's understanding the annoying habits of grocery stores, the essentials are pretty much always around the perimeter and the "junk" in the middle. Think about your store, meat, bakery, dairy and fruit/veggies are probably against outside walls, right? What's in the middle? canned goods, boxed stuff, candy, chips, junk food, sodas... mostly stuff that's not good for a healthy diet. And then they go one step further and put the higher cost/less nutritionally sound foods are eye level (middle of the shelves) and the cheaper/better options on the floor or at the ceiling. The spices/baking isle, tea/coffee section and frozen veggie row are about the only isles I ever walk down. I understand that's not for everyone, and eating boxed dinners (Hamburger Helper) is FAR better than McD's.

Having a list, Sticking to it, and trying to avoid those isles with no quality nutritional items (cookies, chips, sodas) all benefit not only the wallet but the waistline too. :)

We use meal planning as well, though we don't go to the extent of planning our meals around the sales. We have 6 children. We budget 500 every two weeks for groceries. We usually come in around 350 every two weeks, with leftovers to use for lunch the following day almost every day. We used to go to Aldi, and then Walmart, but we don't do that anymore because it turns out the hassle isn't worth the 20-50 we save. For a while we were hitting a local grocer that had great prices, but they have closed (sadly). So we just go to Walmart. We spend a little more (350-380 instead of 330-360) but it's not enough of a price difference to warrant two stops for us, especially since we go together and frequently take the kids with us. Normally we make our meal plan, then I write down what we need, take inventory and cross off what I already have, and organize the rest as close to the format of the store as I can. I'm still learning Walmart's layout, as we've only been going there a couple months. Also, we pack the kids lunches. Sandwich, carrots/celery, and a small snack like goldfish. They get milk at school. Saves us a lot of money in the long run.
